about: Heat in markets and street vending (/market-heat/), November 2026. Each claim is tied to the exact words its source has to hold; stage.js stages the sources in data/inbox/2026-11-market-heat/, verify-sources.yml checks them, and gate.js writes confirmed.json. Figures come from wording already on Common Shade, rechecked here against each source's own text. The Peliyagoda ice-price agreement (Ministry of Fisheries, 2023) is held back: the site's source records that the original notice is no longer online, so it cannot be content-checked. After the first check (28 November 2026): the Bangkok hours figure was dropped (the PDF's text could not be read), the Rewa grant was dropped (PreventionWeb blocked the checker), the Delhi survey claim now cites what the press release holds (over 700 vendors; the exact 721, 80% and 49% are in the full report, not on this page), and the Nagpur claim matches the article's own words.

claims.text: A 2024 report by Greenpeace India and the National Hawkers Federation recorded the experiences of over 700 street vendors through one of India's worst heat waves, and the toll it took on their livelihoods.

In a small trial in a university car park in Pathum Thani, Thailand, artificial canopy materials of the kind used over market stalls lowered air temperature by 1.6-2.3 °C, and dense tree clusters by up to 2.3-3 °C. It measured air temperature, not a working market or anyone's health.
Across 20 shaded and sunlit street sites in Singapore on one very hot afternoon, shade lowered mean radiant temperature by about 10 °C on average, far more than air temperature.
In Los Angeles, reflective-coated roads were cooler on the surface, but people walking above them received more radiant heat; the study's authors paired reflective surfaces with shade.
Heatwaves disrupted schooling for an estimated 171 million students in 2024; South Asia was the most affected region.

In Delhi in 2025, the India Meteorological Department, worker organisations and Greenpeace India set up colour-coded heat boards at vending carts and sent bilingual audio and text alerts on WhatsApp to worker leaders, who passed them on.

In Nagpur in May 2026, temporary green nets over busy junctions kept collapsing in strong winds; commuters and officials asked for durable structures and a long-term heat action plan instead of seasonal fixes.
Occupational heat guidance describes workers watching one another for signs of heat illness as part of protection in hot work; it was written for workplaces, not markets.
